title: Batch cohesion and first-byte latency sensitivity sprint
content:
Purpose:
This sprint explores a novel angle on continuous batching scheduler behavior: how intra-batch "cohesion" (homogeneity of request characteristics inside a batch) correlates with first-byte latency (FBL) for streaming outputs. Many previous notes focus on tail token latency and batch size/timeouts; I wanted a lightweight metric we could compute from traces that explains why sometimes small changes in timeout settings unexpectedly spike the observable first-byte latency for interactive calls.

Background / motivation:
- Product asks for consistent interactive feel for chat-style endpoints (streaming). Users perceive latency as time-to-first-token; p99 token latency is useful but first-byte matters more for perceived responsiveness.
- Continuous batching groups requests opportunistically; this can produce batches that are internally heterogeneous (mix of long & short sequences, cold vs cached kv cache contexts, high vs low priority) which we suspect increases scheduling jitter and stalls streaming emission until the slowest item reaches the token emission stage.
- We introduced a derived metric, "batch_cohesion", to quantify intra-batch similarity and to see if it explains FBL behavior unexplained by batch_size / timeout alone.

Definitions (informal):
- First-byte latency (FBL): time from request arrival to first token emitted to client (ms). Important for streaming endpoints.
- Batch cohesion (BC): a unitless score per batch, 0..1, computed as 1 - normalized variance(feature_vector) where feature_vector includes: sequence_length, estimated_kv_cache_hit_prob, priority_rank. Higher BC => more similar requests. (We compute per-batch using traces; formula in spreadsheet linked above).
- Cohesion-weighted FBL (cwFBL): weighted average of request FBL inside a batch weighted by per-request urgency. Helps see whether bad cohesion disproportionately affects high-urgency requests.

Experiment design summary:
- Workload generator: synthetic trace generator (repo: /tools/trace-gen) that can synthesize: poisson arrivals, controlled bursts, and bimodal seq length distributions (short: 16±4, long: 1024±200). We ran 6 workload modes: steady-low, steady-high, burst-low, burst-high, bimodal-mix, bimodal-high-burst.
- KV cache model: simulate cache hit rates {0%, 30%, 70%}. Cache hits reduce per-request decode time but also change scheduling because cached keys reduce token generation time.
- Scheduler knobs scanned (grid): max_batch_size={8,16,32,64}, max_wait_ms={8,16,32,64}, cohesion_bias={off, low, medium} (cohesion_bias is an instrumented admission heuristic that prefers forming batches with higher predicted cohesion when enabled).
- Other constants: model = open-llama-13B--quant (representative timing profile), 8 GPU pool, priority demotion disabled for this sprint to isolate cohesion effects.
- Metrics captured: per-request FBL (p50/p95/p99), per-request full-response latency, batch_size distribution, per-batch BC, cwFBL, throughput, GPU_util, and cost_estimate (tokens/sec * unit cost).

Key observations (high-level):
1) BC is a strong explanatory variable for FBL variance. For identical scheduler parameters, p99 FBL for low-BC batches is ~1.8–2.3x higher than for high-BC batches. This is consistent across workloads.
2) Under bimodal sequence distributions, naive timeout tuning (increasing max_wait_ms) improves throughput but increases the fraction of low-BC batches (long and short requests coalesced), which increases FBL p95/p99 for short requests.
3) KV cache interacts nonlinearly: at 70% simulated cache hit, low cohesion produces larger FBLs than in zero-cache runs. Hypothesis: cached requests finish earlier in the decode pipeline, but when coalesced with uncached long-gen requests, emission order and KV cache prefetch/pinning cause head-of-line delays for streaming.
4) Enabling cohesion_bias at "low" reduces low-BC batch fraction by ~35% and improves short-request cwFBL p99 by ~28% with <3% throughput loss. "Medium" bias gives more cohesion but starts to hurt throughput by ~8% in peak steady-high mode. Tradeoff sweet spot: low cohesion bias.
5) Purely reducing max_wait_ms to lower FBL for short requests backfires when arrival variability is high: smaller timeouts lead to many very small batches (good for short seqs) but also substantially more scheduler overhead and lower GPU utilization; overall system cost per token goes up. Cohesion bias is cheaper than blindly lowering timeouts.

Representative datapoints (from spreadsheet):
- Bimodal-mix, max_batch=32, max_wait=32ms, kv=30%: p95 FBL = 210ms, p99 FBL = 470ms; low-BC batches (bottom quartile of BC) p99 FBL = 950ms.
- Same workload, cohesion_bias=low: p95 FBL = 180ms, p99 FBL = 320ms, throughput -1.7%.

Why this is different from prior notes: 
- Prior work focused on max_batch and timeout tradeoffs and fairness by age/urgency. This sprint explicitly defines & measures an intra-batch homogeneity metric (BC) and tests a scheduler admission strategy that biases for it. We also emphasize first-byte latency (streaming) which is underexplored in earlier logs.

Low-level trace insights (for engineers):
- When a batch mixes long uncached generations and short cached queries, the first emission gate often waits for the slowest decode buffer to reach the emission boundary due to our current gather->emit pipeline ordering. We saw traces where the short request was ready to emit in 45ms but waited an extra 220–600ms because the batch's final assembly step was serialized behind long-decoder work.
- The KV cache thread pool sometimes gets overloaded when many cached hits coincide in a batch leading to spikes in cache lookup latency; batching them with long uncached requests hides the cache lookup latencies but increases head-of-line FBL for the cached items.

Proposed immediate actions (short-term):
1) Instrumentation: add BC and cwFBL as synthetic metrics in the per-batch telemetry pipeline (Owner: Ethan). Add a per-request "cohesion_tag" to traces for easier filtering (Owner: Jing).
2) Scheduler shim: implement a light-weight cohesion-aware admission heuristic (cohesion_bias=low) in canary branch; limit scope initially to hosted-api small pool. Track throughput and GPU_util to ensure <5% regressions (Owner: Mateo).
3) Pipeline change experiment: enable early emission path for requests predicted to be ready earlier (speculative emit) inside a batch (engineering spike, needs safety guardrails). Risk: may increase interleaving complexity and ordering guarantees. (Owner: Priya).
4) A/B plan: run 2-week canary comparing baseline vs cohesion_bias=low for chat endpoints. KPIs: p95/p99 FBL for short requests, throughput delta, cost_per_token, user-facing error rate. (Owner: Product-run / coordinate with Solutions eng).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How does cohesion interact with function/tool-calling and structured output generation that may have variable decode behavior? Our synthetic model may not fully capture those stalls.
- Is there a simpler proxy than our multi-feature BC to use in production? We need to see if sequence_length alone suffices as a cheap heuristic (initial experiments say "helps but weaker").
- Edge-case: what happens when cohesion_bias leads to request skew (starvation of odd-length requests) under extreme load? Need safety demotion thresholds.

Notes to self / follow-ups:
- Push traces and the cohort analysis notebook to the experiment hub (done).
- Run an additional sweep where cohorting is combined with small dynamic timeouts (e.g., cohesion-aware timeout shortening) to see if we can get both low FBL and throughput.
- Discuss with Platform engineering on exposing cohesion metric to Redwood Console for per-route dashboards if canary shows strong signal.

Appendix (quick checklist):
- [x] Trace generator paramization for bimodal and bursts
- [x] Metric math and spreadsheet calculations
- [ ] Implement cohesion_tag in tracing (Ethan)
- [ ] Cohesion_bias canary patch (Mateo)
- [ ] Early-emission prototype spike (Priya)

End of sprint writeup. Comments welcome — especially from SRE on safety limits and from RD on how to surface BC in the console without overwhelming users with new metrics.
